Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Italian newspapers, an archbishop and civil liberties campaigners expressed shock and revulsion on Monday after photographs were published of sunbathers apparently enjoying a day at the beach just meters from where the bodies of two drowned Roma girls were laid out on the sand. Photographs of the dead Roma girls on a beach caused outrage in Italy. Italian news agency ANSA reported that the incident had occurred on Saturday at the beach of Torregaveta, west of Naples, southern Italy, where the two girls had earlier been swimming in the sea with two other Roma girls. Reports said they had gone to the beach to beg and sell trinkets. Local news reports said the four girls found themselves in trouble amid fierce waves and strong currents. Emergency services responded 10 minutes after a distress call was made from the beach and two lifeguards attended the girls upon hearing their screams. Two of them were pulled to safety but rescuers failed to reach the other two in time to save them.  Watch why the photos have generated anger » . The Web site of the Archbishop of Naples said the girls were cousins named Violetta and Cristina, aged 12 and 13. Their bodies were eventually laid out on the sand under beach towels to await collection by police. Photographs show sunbathers in bikinis and swimming trunks sitting close to where the girls' feet can be seen poking out from under the towels concealing their bodies. A photographer who took photos at the scene told CNN the mood among sunbathers had been one of indifference. Other photos show police officers lifting the bodies into coffins and carrying them away past bathers reclined on sun loungers. "While the lifeless bodies of the girls were still on the sand, there were those who carried on sunbathing or having lunch just a few meters away," Italian newspaper La Repubblica reported. Corriere della Sera said that a crowd of curious onlookers that had formed around the bodies quickly dispersed. "Few left the beach or abandoned their sunbathing. When the police from the mortuary arrived an hour later with coffins, the two girls were carried away between bathers stretched out in the sun." The incident also attracted condemnation from the Archbishop of Naples, Cardinal Crecenzio Seppe. "Indifference is not an emotion for human beings," Seppe wrote in his parish blog. "To turn the other way or to mind your own business can sometimes be more devastating than the events that occur." Recent weeks have seen heightened tensions between Italian authorities and the country's Roma minority amid a crackdown by Silvo Berlusconi's government targeting illegal immigrants and talk by government officials of a "Roma emergency" that has seen the 150,000-strong migrant group blamed for rising street crime. That has provided justification for police raids on Roma camps and controversial government plans to fingerprint all Roma -- an act condemned by the European Parliament and United Nations officials as a clear act of racial discrimination. Popular resentment against Romanies has also seen Roma camps near Naples attacked and set on fire with petrol bombs by local residents. In a statement published on its Web site, the Italian civil liberties group EveryOne said Saturday's drowning had occurred in an atmosphere of "racism and horror" and cast doubt on the reported version of events, suggesting that it appeared unusual for the four girls to wade into the sea, apparently casting modesty aside and despite being unable to swim. "The most shocking aspect of all this is the attitude of the people on the beach," the statement said. "No one appears the slightest upset at the sight and presence of the children's dead bodies on the beach: they carry on swimming, sunbathing, sipping soft drinks and chatting." CNN's Jennifer Eccleston contributed to this report.

# Beach Tragedy Sparks National Outrage in Italy

Public figures across Italy—including newspaper editors, a high-ranking church official, and human rights advocates—reacted with disgust on Monday when images surfaced showing beachgoers casually tanning mere feet away from the covered corpses of two young Roma girls who had drowned.

According to the Italian news service ANSA, the tragedy unfolded Saturday at Torregaveta beach, located west of Naples in southern Italy. The victims had been swimming alongside two other Roma girls, reportedly having come to the shore to panhandle and hawk small goods to tourists. Local accounts indicate the group of four got caught in dangerous rip currents and rough surf.

Although lifeguards rushed to the scene after hearing the girls' cries for help—arriving roughly ten minutes after receiving an emergency call—they only managed to rescue two of the four. The other two perished.

Per information posted on the Naples Archdiocese's website, the deceased were identified as cousins Violetta, 12, and Cristina, 13. Beach towels were used to cover their bodies as they awaited pickup by authorities, but photographs later showed their bare feet visible beneath the coverings, with sunbathers in swimwear lounging nearby, seemingly unbothered.

A photojournalist present at the scene described to CNN an atmosphere of general apathy among beach visitors. Additional images captured officers loading the girls' bodies into caskets and transporting them past rows of people relaxing on beach chairs.

The Italian daily La Repubblica noted that "while the girls' bodies remained motionless on the sand, nearby beachgoers continued their tanning and picnicking as if nothing had happened." Meanwhile, Corriere della Sera reported that although a group of curious spectators initially gathered, most soon returned to their leisure activities. "Barely anyone left the beach or paused their sunbathing," the paper wrote, adding that when mortuary staff finally arrived an hour later with coffins, the girls were carried out past sunbathers who never moved from their loungers.

Naples' Archbishop, Cardinal Crescenzio Sepe, publicly condemned the incident via his parish blog, writing: "Apathy has no place in human nature. Looking away or minding one's own business can sometimes cause more harm than the tragedy itself."

This incident comes amid escalating friction between Italian officials and the nation's Roma population, fueled by Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi's immigration crackdown. Government rhetoric about a so-called "Roma emergency" has placed blame on this ethnic minority—numbering roughly 150,000 people—for a perceived increase in crime. This narrative has been used to justify police sweeps of Roma settlements and a controversial fingerprinting initiative targeting all Roma individuals, a policy denounced by both the European Parliament and UN representatives as blatantly discriminatory.

Anti-Roma sentiment has also manifested violently, with residents near Naples firebombing Roma encampments using petrol bombs.

The advocacy organization EveryOne issued a statement asserting that the drowning took place against a backdrop of "racism and horror." The group also questioned the official narrative, finding it implausible that the girls—who reportedly couldn't swim—would have entered the water at all. "What's most disturbing here is how the beach crowd behaved," the statement read. "Nobody seemed remotely disturbed by the children's bodies lying there—people just kept swimming, tanning, drinking sodas, and talking among themselves."

*Additional reporting by CNN's Jennifer Eccleston.*

# Tragedy at Torregaveta: Deaths of Two Roma Children Expose Deep-Rooted Prejudice in Italy

## The Incident

In late July 2025, tragedy struck at Torregaveta beach near Naples, Italy, when two young cousins from the Roma community—reportedly aged around 11 and 12—drowned in the sea. The children, who had been part of a group visiting the popular coastal spot, got into difficulty in the water. Despite the presence of numerous beachgoers nearby, rescue efforts came too late to save them.

## A Disturbing Public Response

What has drawn the most significant national and international attention, however, is not merely the tragedy itself but the reaction of bystanders in its aftermath. According to multiple accounts and witness testimonies, many people on the beach reportedly continued their normal activities—sunbathing, swimming, and socializing—seemingly undisturbed by the unfolding tragedy just meters away. Some reports suggest that beachgoers showed little urgency in assisting or even acknowledging the emergency, while others allegedly resumed leisure activities shortly after the bodies were recovered.

This apparent indifference sparked outrage across Italian media and social platforms, with many drawing a direct connection to the victims' Roma identity. Critics argued that the muted, detached response reflected a broader societal apathy—or worse, prejudice—toward Roma communities, who have long faced marginalization, discrimination, and social exclusion throughout Italy and much of Europe.

## Official Reactions

The incident prompted responses from various Italian political figures and institutions, though reactions were notably mixed. Some officials offered condolences and called for solidarity, emphasizing that the tragedy of two children's deaths should transcend ethnic or social divisions. Others faced criticism for what advocates described as tepid or perfunctory statements that failed to address the underlying issue of anti-Roma sentiment highlighted by the incident.

Local authorities in the Campania region, where Torregaveta is located, faced questions about beach safety measures and emergency response protocols, though the controversy surrounding public reaction has largely overshadowed discussions of logistical failures.

## Human Rights Organizations Speak Out

Human rights groups and Roma advocacy organizations were quick to condemn what they characterized as a shocking display of dehumanization. Organizations focused on combating anti-Gypsyism and racial discrimination pointed to the incident as a stark illustration of how deeply entrenched anti-Roma prejudice remains in Italian society.

Advocates argued that had the victims belonged to a different ethnic or social background, the public and media response would likely have been markedly different—characterized by greater collective mourning, urgency, and empathy. They called on the Italian government to take concrete action against discrimination faced by Roma communities, including improved access to social services, education, and protection from systemic marginalization.

Several organizations also called for an independent investigation into the events at Torregaveta, urging authorities to examine not only the circumstances of the drowning but also the conduct of witnesses and beach staff during the emergency.

## A Reflection of Broader Issues

The deaths of the two children have become a flashpoint for renewed debate about the treatment of Roma populations in Italy, a country where Roma and Sinti communities have historically faced housing segregation, employment discrimination, and social stigmatization. Critics argue that incidents like this reveal an uncomfortable truth: that certain lives are perceived as less worthy of collective grief and immediate action than others.

As investigations continue and public debate intensifies, the tragedy at Torregaveta has become more than a story of accidental drowning—it has emerged as a painful symbol of the human rights challenges still facing marginalized communities across Italy and Europe.
